text: A non-competitive inhibitor binds at a different site from the substrate. It binds reversibly at a site other than the active site, and that binding changes the shape of the active site, so the active site is no longer complementary to the substrate. Watch: the inhibitor seats at the other site, the cleft distorts, a substrate arrives and cannot seat. Adding more substrate cannot restore the uninhibited maximum rate, because it does not compete for the inhibitor's binding site. In the simplified model drawn here, Vmax decreases, increasing substrate concentration does not restore it, and K M is unchanged: read from its own, lower, half Vmax, it comes out at the same concentration. When the inhibitor leaves, the active site returns to its shape and activity comes back.
